readerTitle: Why the owner who stopped searching early won
caseNote: 가상 사례 (생활용품 소매점, 금속 부품 공장, 소프트웨어 회사) + 실제 연구 (Herbert Simon의 satisficing, Schwartz·Iyengar의 maximizer 연구)
insight: 모든 결정에서 최고를 찾는 데도 비용이 든다. 먼저 '충분히 좋은' 기준을 정하고 그 기준을 넘는 첫 선택지를 고르면, 탐색에 드는 시간과 주의를 정말 중요한 결정에 쓸 수 있다.
misconception: 선택지를 더 많이 비교할수록 언제나 더 좋은 결정이 나온다. 최고가 아닌 것을 고르면 타협이다.

sources.text: Simon, H. A. (1956). Rational Choice and the Structure of the Environment. Psychological Review, 63(2), 129–138.

Schwartz, B., Ward, A., Monterosso, J., Lyubomirsky, S., White, K., & Lehman, D. R. (2002). Maximizing versus satisficing: Happiness is a matter of choice. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 83(5), 1178–1197.
Iyengar, S. S., Wells, R. E., & Schwartz, B. (2006). Doing better but feeling worse: Looking for the "best" job undermines satisfaction. Psychological Science, 17(2), 143–150.
Lena, Raj, 소프트웨어 회사 사례와 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Herbert Simon이 'satisficing'(satisfy + suffice)이라는 말을 1956년 Psychological Review 논문에서 소개했다는 점을 1차 출처로 확인하세요. 일부 자료는 1955년 논문(A Behavioral Model of Rational Choice)을 함께 언급합니다. 카드에는 '1950s'로만 적었습니다.
Schwartz 외(2002): maximizer 성향이 강한 사람일수록 행복감·만족도가 낮고 후회가 크다고 보고했습니다. 상관관계 연구라는 점을 고려해 카드에는 'tended to'로 적었습니다.
Iyengar 외(2006): 졸업 예정자 중 maximizer가 더 높은 초봉의 일자리를 얻었지만 결과에 덜 만족했다는 내용입니다. 구체적 수치(약 20% 높은 초봉)는 카드에 넣지 않았습니다. 게시 전 원문으로 확인하세요.
Lena와 Raj의 사례 수치(견적 4개/14개, 2일/7주, 운송비 3% 절감)는 모두 가상입니다. 계산이 필요한 수치는 없습니다.

cards.title: Why the owner who stopped searching early won
body: Same week, same problem. Lena runs a homeware store. Raj runs a small metal-parts workshop. Both needed a new supplier.
Lena decided in two days. Raj compared quotes for seven weeks and found a slightly cheaper deal.
By the end of the season, Lena was the one who had come out ahead.

image.label: Two owners: one with a short checklist, one buried in quotes
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눈 일러스트. 왼쪽은 소매점 주인이 체크 표시 3개짜리 짧은 목록을 들고 웃으며 박스를 받는 모습. 오른쪽은 작은 공장 사무실에서 주인이 견적서 더미에 파묻혀 달력을 넘기는 모습. 실제 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: Gift bags before the holiday rush.
body: You're Lena. Your gift-bag supplier just closed, and the holiday season starts in three weeks. Bags are a small cost, and you can switch suppliers next year.
How do you choose a new one?

options.text: Get quotes from every supplier you can find and pick the cheapest
options.feedback: You might save a few cents per bag, but the search eats days you need for holiday stock, and the cheapest quote may arrive late.

options.text: Decide three must-haves first, then take the first supplier that meets all of them
options.feedback: You give up the chance of the very best deal but get a solid one fast. For a small, reversible choice, that trade is usually worth it.

options.text: Ask the first two suppliers you find and pick the cheaper one
options.feedback: Fast, which is right here. But without clear must-haves, "cheaper" can hide slow delivery or flimsy bags.

cards.title: Two searches, side by side.
body: Raj's new freight carrier really was cheaper. But while he searched, two big orders shipped late with his old, unreliable carrier, and one customer moved part of its business elsewhere.

breakdown.label: Lena's bar
breakdown.detail: Under budget, delivery in a week, recycled paper

breakdown.label: Raj's search
breakdown.detail: No bar set, kept looking for the best

breakdown.label: Raj's cost
breakdown.detail: Saved about 3% on freight, lost late orders

cards.title: Good enough vs best
body: In the 1950s, economist Herbert Simon gave Lena's approach a name: **satisficing**, a mix of *satisfy* and *suffice*. You set a bar in advance and choose the first option that clears it.
The opposite is **maximizing**: keep searching until you're sure you've found the best.
Simon's point was that real decision-makers have limited time and attention. Searching for the best isn't free, so a good-enough choice made on time often beats the best choice made late.

image.label: A bar line with options; the first one above it is chosen
image.brief: 가로로 늘어선 선택지 막대들 위에 점선으로 'Good enough' 기준선. 기준선을 처음 넘는 막대에 체크 표시, 그 뒤의 막대들은 흐리게 처리하고 아래에 'Time spent searching' 화살표가 길게 이어짐.

cards.title: Every extra option costs more and adds less.
body: The first few options you check teach you a lot. The tenth rarely does. Meanwhile, each one costs time, attention and delay.

Research suggests the habit has a personal cost too. In studies by Barry Schwartz and colleagues, people who tended to maximize reported less happiness and more regret. In one study of graduating students, maximizers landed jobs with higher starting pay but felt worse about their choices.
Doing slightly better on paper can still mean doing worse overall.

cards.title: Save your best search for the big calls.
body: Satisficing isn't a rule for everything. Search harder when a choice is **costly, hard to undo, and the options differ a lot**.
If Raj were buying a machine he'd run for fifteen years, weeks of comparison would make sense. A freight contract he could change in a month did not deserve the same effort.
The skill is sorting decisions: most are gift bags, a few are machines.

cards.title: Good enough depends on where you set the bar.
body: Satisficing only works if you set the bar *before* you look. Set it after, and it quietly drops to match whatever you found first. That's settling, not satisficing.
A bar set too low also hides real risks. "Delivers on time" might matter more than you assumed.
Adjust the bar when the evidence says so: raise it if many options clear it easily, and rethink it if none do.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: You run a six-person software company. You need a tool to manage customer support emails. Plans are monthly, and you can cancel anytime. There are dozens of options.
What's the smartest way to choose?

options.text: Trial the top nine tools for a month each, then compare
options.feedback: You'd learn a lot about support tools and lose most of a year. Customers keep emailing while you test.

options.text: List three must-haves, trial the first tool that claims them, keep it if it works
options.feedback: A cheap, reversible choice gets a quick, solid answer. If it fails your bar, you cancel and try the next one.

options.text: Pick whatever tool the biggest company in your market uses
options.feedback: Fast, and probably decent. But a tool built for a 500-person team may fail your own must-haves on price or setup.

cards.title: Decide what's good enough before you start looking.
body: Most decisions need a clear bar, not the perfect option. Keep your long searches for the few choices that are big and hard to undo.
**Try it today:** pick one decision you've been putting off. Write down three must-haves, then choose the first option that meets them.
